 Michelle R. Fajman, director of the Lake County Board of Elections and Registration, describes the number of voters on the first day of early voting at the Lake County Government Center in Crown Point on Tuesday, Oct 6, 2026. (John Smierciak/for the Post-Tribune) 
 By Maya Wilkins | Post-Tribune PUBLISHED: November 7, 2026 at 9:00 AM CST Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... Lake County saw some positive numbers following the 2026 general election, the county’s top election official said.
 However, she still wants to see more people at the polls.
 “We did better,” Michelle Fajman, Lake County’s elections and registrations, told the Post-Tribune. “We’re three percentage points higher, which is good. It’s not as much as — being the election administrator — I’d like to see, but it is better, and more people are having a say in their elections.”
 According to unofficial election results, voter turnout was 39.52% in this week’s general election, up from 36.92% in the 2022 midterm general election.
 In the 2024 presidential election, Lake County saw a 57.25% voter turnout, according to previous Lake County election records.
 Fajman said early voting was up this year compared to previous years, seeing 56,034 voters in that time. On Election Day, 85,292 county residents voted.
 According to Post-Tribune archives, Fajman said the Friday before early voting ended, about 46,000 people voted, up from 30,000 at the same time four years ago. Mail-in voting was down by about 5,000 votes, Fajman said, but still up 10,000 from 2022.
 Fajman said the county rejected about 50 mail-in ballots on Election Day because people wrote the incorrect date on their ballot.
 “The only cure process on that is the voter must come to Crown Point, pick up an affidavit stating that the ballot has been rejected, and then they can go all the way back to their polling place to recast a vote,” Fajman said.
 According to Ballotpedia, Indiana voters can cure their mail-in ballot after Election Day.
 Fajman believes voter turnout could be higher because of several local issues.
 “The prices of gas, the prices of stuff at the stores, and then from what you hear in the paper about the war (with Iran) could have been some of it,” she said. “Hopefully it’s people just taking more of an active role in their communities, and this becomes lifelong commitments for them as they continue to vote.”
 Nationwide, Democrats saw big wins, and Lake County Democratic Chair Mike Repay said higher voter turnout helped the party.
 “Good voter turnout is good for government,” Repay said. “The more voters and the more input we get from voters, the better we govern, I believe.”
 Repay also believes that issues like affordability helped get people out to the polls this year.
 Going into municipal elections and the presidential election, Repay said the party has learned that communication from candidates can help voter turnout. He said they also saw a lot of success from first-time candidates this year.
 “I think that taught us a lesson to not be a closed-off organization but to be an open organization … and we’ll continue that into the municipal (elections) for sure,” Repay said.
 Lake County Republican Party Chair Randy Niemeyer, who was re-elected to his Lake County Council 7th District seat, was unable to respond to a request about what lessons his party took from voter turnout.
 Official state voter turnout numbers are not yet available, but according to Indiana Voters’ online portal, 568,317 people voted on Election Day, and more than 1.04 million people voted in total. Unofficial numbers have voter statewide turnout at 42%.
 Julia Vaughn, executive director of Common Cause Indiana, said several counties were “key to significant results” this year, including Hamilton County in the north suburbs of Indianapolis. Democratic State Senator J.D. Ford defeated U.S. Rep. Victoria Spartz, R-5th, in the congressional district encompassing those suburbs and stretching northeast.
 “That was very palpable,” she said. “We had election protection volunteers up there on Tuesday, and they were reporting back to me at 6:00 that there were lines an hour and a half long of people waiting to cast their ballots.”
 Vaughn believes a combination of national and local issues motivated people to vote in the midterm elections. She hopes voters continue to be motivated, especially ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
 “That’s the only way they’re going to have a say in our government at both the federal and state levels,” Vaughn said.
 Government corruption and affordability, specifically with utilities, rank at the top of voter issues, Vaughn said. She believes legislators that were “seen as too friendly to utility companies” suffered because of voters’ frustrations with high utility bills, especially as more data center development continues statewide,
 “Hoosiers are, I think as they expressed through their votes on Tuesday, concerned about the direction of our country and our state,” Vaughn said. “I think that sort of discontent with the way things are going and a real call for change is what motivated voters this election season. Let’s hope that politicians are listening and will provide the public policy and change that Hoosiers are calling for.”
 mwilkins@chicagotribune.com
